title: Identify, describe, compare, classify, explore shape and motion in 2-and 3-dimensional shapes in different contexts

lessons.title: Flat shapes and solid shapes
lessons.html:
2-D and 3-D shapes around us

Shapes are all around the workplace. Knowing their names and features helps you measure, pack and stack things correctly.

2-dimensional (flat) shapes

A 2-D shape is flat. It has length and width but no thickness. You can draw it on paper.

ShapeFeaturesWhere you see it
Square4 equal sides, 4 right anglesFloor tiles
Rectangle4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 right anglesTop of a pallet, a door
Triangle3 sides, 3 cornersWarning signs
CircleRound, every point the same distance from the centreProhibition signs, drain covers

3-dimensional (solid) shapes

A 3-D shape has length, width and height. It takes up space and you can hold or fill it.

  • Cube: 6 square faces, like a dice or some cartons.
  • Rectangular prism (box shape): 6 rectangle faces, like a carton of meat cuts or a bale.
  • Cylinder: 2 round faces and a curved side, like a drum, a pipe or a silo.
  • Cone: a round base and a point, like the top of a silo hopper or a heap of grain.
  • Sphere: completely round, like a ball or an egg (nearly).

Faces, edges and corners

A face is a flat side. An edge is where two faces meet. A corner (vertex) is where edges meet. A carton has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.

lessons.title: Comparing and sorting shapes
lessons.html:
Comparing shapes

We compare shapes by size, number of sides and how they fit together. This is useful when packing, stacking and storing.

Sorting by features

You can classify shapes into groups:

  • Shapes with straight sides (squares, rectangles, triangles) and shapes with curves (circles).
  • Solid shapes that stack well (cubes and boxes) and those that roll (cylinders and spheres).
  • Shapes with right angles (square corners) and those without.

Why boxes stack well

Cartons are box-shaped because their flat faces and square corners fit tightly together with no gaps. This saves space in a cold room or on a truck. Round drums leave gaps between them, and they can roll. Drums must be stored upright or chocked so they cannot roll and injure someone.

Similar and different sizes

Two cartons can have the same shape but different sizes. A 5 kg carton and a 10 kg carton might both be box-shaped, but one is bigger. When you stack, put the bigger, heavier cartons at the bottom and smaller, lighter ones on top. This keeps the stack stable.

Symmetry

A shape is symmetrical if you can fold it in half and both sides match. A beef carcass split down the backbone gives two sides that are nearly mirror images. Many safety signs are also symmetrical.

Angles

A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a page. Check that a stack is straight by looking that the sides make right angles with the floor. A leaning stack can fall.

lessons.title: Position, movement and plans
lessons.html:
Describing where things are

At work you often need to describe where something is or how to get there. Use clear position words: left, right, in front of, behind, above, below, next to, between.

Example: 'The first aid box is on the wall to the left of the change room door, above the hand basin.'

Reading a simple plan

A floor plan is a drawing of a building from above. It shows rooms, doors, machines and emergency exits as flat shapes. On a plan:

  • Rectangles often show rooms, tables or machines.
  • Gaps or arcs in walls show doors.
  • Green arrows or the word EXIT show escape routes.
  • A small arrow marked N shows north.

Look at the evacuation plan in your workplace. Find where you work, the nearest exit and the assembly point.

Movement: turning and moving

Things can move in different ways:

  • Slide (move in a straight line): a carton on a conveyor belt.
  • Turn (rotate): a wheel, a fan or a mixer paddle. A full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn is 180 degrees and a quarter turn is 90 degrees.
  • Flip (reflect): turning a carton over so the label faces up.

Safety with moving parts

Rotating parts, such as augers in grain handling and shafts on machines, can catch clothing and hands. Never reach into a moving machine. Keep guards in place and make sure the machine is switched off and locked out before anyone cleans it.

Key points

  • 2-D shapes are flat; 3-D shapes have length, width and height.
  • A box shape has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.
  • Box shapes stack well; cylinders and spheres can roll.
  • Use clear position words and floor plans to describe locations.
  • Movement can be a slide, turn or flip; a quarter turn is 90 degrees.
  • Never reach into rotating machine parts.
